source.title: Billiard Dynamics: A Survey with the Emphasis on Open Problems

accepted.question_text: Let Y be a smooth, strictly convex planar billiard table, and let Φ be the annular phase space of its billiard map φ. An invariant circle is a φ-invariant noncontractible topological circle Γ⊂Φ, and Y is called integrable when the union of invariant circles in Φ has nonempty interior. Is every such integrable billiard table necessarily an ellipse?

evidence.quote: Definition 1. A billiard table Y is integrable if the union of invariant circles in the phase space has nonempty interior.
Problem 1. Ellipses are the only integrable billiard tables.

accepted.question_text: Construct a planar billiard table with positive entropy in either of the following regularity classes: (a) a strictly convex table whose boundary is C1-smooth, or (b) a convex table whose boundary is C2-smooth.

evidence.quote: By the (metric) entropy of a billiard we mean the entropy of the Liouville measure.
Problem 2. a) Construct a strictly convex C1-smooth billiard table with positive entropy. b) Construct a convex C2-smooth billiard table with positive entropy.

accepted.question_text: Let Y be a smooth, strictly convex planar billiard table, let Φ be the phase space of its billiard map, let 𝒫⊂Φ be the set of all periodic points, and let 𝒫_n⊂Φ be the set of periodic points of period n. With respect to the invariant Liouville measure μ on Φ, is μ(𝒫)=0? Equivalently, is μ(𝒫_n)=0 for every n?

evidence.quote: Let  ⊂ Φ (resp.  n ⊂ Φ) be the set of periodic points (resp. periodic points of period n).
Problem 3. Let Y be any Birkhoff billiard table. i) Prove that µ() = 0. ii) Prove that µ(n) = 0 for all n.

accepted.question_text: A semi-dispersive billiard table is obtained from a polygon by replacing some sides by smooth boundary components that are convex inward, while any remaining straight sides are neutral components; a semi-dispersive polygon is the special case where the dispersive components are circular arcs. Is every semi-dispersive billiard table hyperbolic? Is every semi-dispersive polygon hyperbolic?

evidence.quote: These are the semi-dispersive billiard tables. In the absence of neutral components, we speak of dispersive billiard tables.
Problem 4. i) Is every semi-dispersive billiard table hyperbolic? ii) Is every semi-dispersive polygon hyperbolic?

accepted.question_text: For a dispersive billiard table Y, let f_Y(n) denote the number of periodic orbits of the billiard map whose period is at most n. Does the exponential growth rate h = lim_{n→∞} (log f_Y(n))/n exist?

evidence.quote: Let fY (n) be the number of periodic orbits, whose period is less than or equal to n.
Problem 5. Does the limit below exist? h = limn→∞ log fY (n) / n (2.2)

accepted.question_text: Assume that for a dispersive billiard table Y the limit h = lim_{n→∞} (log f_Y(n))/n exists, where f_Y(n) counts periodic orbits of period at most n. Is this growth-rate constant h equal to the topological entropy of the billiard map?

evidence.quote: Problem 6. If the limit in equation (2.2) does exist, is h the topological entropy of the billiard map?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an irrational polygon, meaning a polygon whose side angles are not all rational multiples of π, whose billiard dynamics is nonergodic?

evidence.quote: It is rational if the angles between its sides are of the form πm/n.
Problem 8. Give an example of an irrational, nonergodic polygon3.

evidence.quote: Problem 10. Does every polygon have a periodic orbit?

accepted.question_text: For an irrational polygon P, let f_P(ℓ) denote the number of periodic bands of billiard orbits of length at most ℓ. Find nontrivial upper and lower bounds for f_P(ℓ).
accepted.context_brief: Counting periodic bands in irrational polygons

evidence.quote: Denote by fP (￿) the number of periodic bands of length at most ￿. This is a counting function of periodic orbits in polygons.
Problem 11. Find nontrivial (upper and lower) bounds on fP for irrational polygons.

accepted.question_text: For a rational polygon P, let f_P(ℓ) be the number of periodic bands of length at most ℓ, and let c_*(P) and c^*(P) be constants giving quadratic lower and upper bounds c_*(P)ℓ^2 ≤ f_P(ℓ) ≤ c^*(P)ℓ^2 for all sufficiently large ℓ. Find effective estimates for these constants.
